page: Amazon Web Services r9g.8xlarge is a memory-optimized instance powered by AWS-designed arm64 Graviton processors on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture. The instance provides 32 dedicated physical cores running at 3.3 GHz without simultaneous multithreading, mapping directly to 32 vCPUs. It is configured with 256.0 GB of system memory, maintaining an 8:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio with 8.0 GB of RAM allocated per physical core.

Network infrastructure on the r9g.8xlarge delivers a baseline bandwidth of 17 Gbps. This instance type includes no local bundled instance storage, requiring network-attached storage such as Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS) for persistent data needs. Additionally, it features no dedicated hardware accelerators or GPUs, and comes with zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Due to its high memory density and single-threaded dedicated core architecture, the instance provides strong resource predictability and architectural cost efficiency for arm64-compatible environments. It is well matched for memory-intensive enterprise workloads, including in-memory databases, caching layers, distributed analytics, and large-scale data processing pipelines.
description: Amazon Web Services r9g.8xlarge is a memory-optimized instance featuring 32 dedicated arm64 cores running at 3.3 GHz via AWS Graviton processors on the Nitro hypervisor. With one thread per physical core, it eliminates multithreading contention across its 32 vCPUs. The server is provisioned with 256.0 GB of memory, equating to 8.0 GB of RAM per vCPU, and is supported by a 17 Gbps baseline network interface. The instance features no local NVMe storage and no GPU accelerators, relying on network-attached storage for persistence. Built for environments requiring heavy memory capacities per compute unit, r9g.8xlarge provides high memory-to-core density and predictable CPU performance on the arm64 architecture. It is suited for in-memory databases, Redis and Memcached caching tiers, real-time analytics engines, and enterprise data processing workloads.
